qs.q: All of the following are zoophilic dermatophytes EXCEPT ONE:
qs.e: Epidermophyton floccosum is an anthropophilic dermatophyte, meaning it primarily infects humans. Trichophyton mentagrophytes, Microsporum canis, and Trichophyton verrucosum are common zoophilic dermatophytes, primarily associated with animal hosts.

qs.q: Dermatophyte infection is most often associated with:
o: Adherence of organism to perspiration-moist skin
qs.e: Dermatophytes thrive in moist, warm areas of the skin where they adhere and cause superficial infections.

qs.q: All of the following dermatophytes are responsible for nail infections EXCEPT:
o: Trichophyton rubrum, a common cause of onychomycosis.
Microsporum canis, typically associated with animal‑derived skin infections.
Epidermophyton floccosum, frequently implicated in nail disease.
Trichophyton mentagrophytes, another frequent nail pathogen.
qs.e: Microsporum species typically infect hair and skin but not nails, whereas Trichophyton and Epidermophyton are common causes of onychomycosis.
qs.s: Weekly Year 3: Medical Mycology Exam - August 21, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: All of the following dermatophytes are frequently responsible for nail infections (onychomycosis) EXCEPT:
qs.e: Trichophyton rubrum, T. mentagrophytes, and Epidermophyton floccosum are common causes of onychomycosis. Microsporum canis is primarily associated with tinea capitis and tinea corporis, not typically nail infections.
qs.s: Weekly Year 3: Medical Mycology Exam - August 14, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: Which of the following dermatophytes does NOT have the spore form characteristic called Microconidia?
qs.e: Epidermophyton floccosum produces only macroconidia and lacks microconidia, which is a key distinguishing laboratory feature.

ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Dermatophytes are fungi that invade keratinised skin, hair and nails, causing tinea infections. They trigger a cellular immune response and can present with characteristic ring‑shaped lesions.

sections.p: Dermatophytes are filamentous fungi that digest keratin. They are classified into three genera—Trichophyton, Microsporum and Epidermophyton—each with distinct epidemiology.
b: Spread by direct contact or fomites

sections.p: They produce hyaline, septate hyphae and macroconidia whose shape helps species identification.
b: Macroconidia: club‑shaped in Microsporum, spindle‑shaped in Trichophyton
Require keratin for growth; cannot invade deep tissue

sections.p: Spores are shed from infected skin, hair or nails and survive on surfaces for months, allowing spread in households, schools and communal showers.
b: Animal reservoirs (e.g., cats, dogs) for zoophilic species

sections.p: Dermatophytes cause tinea corporis, tinea cruris, tinea pedis, tinea unguium and tinea capitis, each defined by location and clinical pattern.
b: Tinea capitis: scaly, alopecic patches, common in children
Tinea unguium: nail thickening, subungual debris
Inflammatory variants (e.g., erythema migrans‑like) may mimic bacterial infection

sections.p: Clinical appearance guides initial suspicion; laboratory confirmation uses microscopy and culture, but rapid point‑of‑care tests are useful when resources are limited.
b: Wood's lamp: bright fluorescence in Microsporum infections

t.b: Does the sample contain fungal hyphae? Positive confirms dermatophyte infection.
What species is present? Species guides epidemiology and treatment duration.
Is there fluorescence? Positive suggests Microsporum spp.; negative does not rule out infection.

sections.p: First‑line therapy is topical azoles for limited disease; oral agents are required for scalp, nail or extensive infection. Education reduces reinfection.
b: Topical terbinafine or azoles: inhibit ergosterol synthesis, good for tinea corporis/cruris/pedis
Oral terbinafine or itraconazole: preferred for tinea capitis and onychomycosis; avoid griseofulvin in hepatic disease
Keep skin dry, avoid sharing towels, treat pets if zoonotic source

sections.p: Focus on pattern recognition, diagnostic steps, and rationale for drug choice.
b: Ring‑shaped, scaly plaque with central clearing → tinea corporis
Hair loss with black dot patches in a child → tinea capitis, confirm with KOH
Nail dystrophy without trauma → consider tinea unguium; culture if available

whenToSeekHelp: Systemic symptoms (fever, chills) with extensive skin involvement
Immunocompromised patient with widespread dermatophyte infection

faq.q: Why do dermatophytes only affect skin, hair and nails?
faq.a: They produce keratinases that digest keratin, the main protein in these tissues, but lack enzymes to invade deeper layers.

faq.q: Can a bacterial infection look like a dermatophyte infection?
faq.a: Yes, erythematous, scaly lesions can mimic cellulitis; KOH microscopy helps differentiate.

faq.q: What if culture facilities are unavailable?
faq.a: A positive KOH exam plus typical clinical features is sufficient to start treatment.
